screens.title: State Management Fundamentals in Flutter
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll make sense of application state and why a simple setState call becomes fragile as apps grow. State means any data that changes while your app runs and that affects what the user sees. setState is fine for local widget state, but when several widgets need the same data, passing values down repeatedly, also called prop drilling, makes code hard to follow and maintain. Provider offers a lightweight, Flutter-friendly approach built on InheritedWidget. You define a model that extends ChangeNotifier, make it available with a Provider placed higher in the tree, and read or watch that model in descendant widgets. This pattern separates UI from business logic and helps you avoid duplicated updates or tangled callbacks. For example, a counter model exposes a count and increment method; the UI listens for changes and rebuilds when notifyListeners is called. A common pitfall is forgetting notifyListeners or using read where you need watch. Over this chapter you'll learn ChangeNotifier structure, Provider placement, Consumer and Selector use, and a hands-on to-do app. By the end you will be able to choose Provider for moderate complexity apps and understand when finer-grained tools might be required. How could this pattern clean up one of your own widgets?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives will guide our work with Provider and ChangeNotifier. First, you'll explain why effective state management is necessary beyond setState, identifying where prop drilling and duplicated update logic create bugs. This objective matters because recognizing when to centralize state helps you choose the right pattern early. Second, you'll understand Provider's core principles: that Provider wraps an InheritedWidget, that ChangeNotifier is the observable model, and that Provider exposes instances to descendants. A concrete example is creating a CounterModel and observing how a single provider instance updates several widgets. Third, you'll implement ChangeNotifier to model observable data, including calling notifyListeners after state changes. This skill is essential to write models that correctly trigger UI rebuilds. Finally, you'll use Provider, Consumer, Selector, and context. watch/read to react to changes efficiently and avoid unnecessary rebuilds. For instance, Selector allows you to rebuild a specific widget only when a selected piece of state changes, improving performance. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress and fix common mistakes like forgetting notifyListeners or using read in a build method.

screens.title: What is application state and where setState falls short
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define application state and examine why local setState quickly becomes fragile. State is any data that can change while the app runs and that affects the UI: user input, network results, theme toggles, or a shopping cart. Local state lives inside a single StatefulWidget and can be handled with setState. But when the same data is needed by many widgets at different depths, passing values and callbacks down the tree — called prop drilling — creates tightly coupled components. This coupling makes maintenance harder, testing more painful, and refactors risky because many widgets rely on the same plumbing. Consider a user profile name that must appear in the app bar, a settings page, and a drawer; updating it via setState alone forces you to bubble callbacks through several layers. A centralized observable model solves this by providing a single source of truth. Concrete example: replacing multiple setState callbacks with a ChangeNotifier model that holds the name and calls notifyListeners when it updates. Misconception to check: setState is not inherently bad — it is the right tool for local widget state such as animations or temporary form field values. The key takeaway: use setState for local concerns and choose a Provider-style pattern when state is shared across unrelated widgets, to reduce duplication and make updates predictable. Which piece of your app would be easier to refactor with a central model?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › State vs setState
Definition

Application state

State is any mutable data that influences UI. Local state belongs to one widget. Shared state must be accessible by many widgets.

Problems when misapplied
  • Prop drilling increases coupling and reduces readability.
  • Multiple setState calls across widgets can create inconsistent views.
  • Harder to test and to reuse UI components when state is embedded everywhere.
Key Takeaway

Local setState is fine for isolated widgets. When data needs to cross boundaries, centralize it with an observable model to keep the UI consistent.

Concrete example

Imagine a logged-in user's display name used in an AppBar, Settings screen, and a Profile widget. With setState you'd pass the name through several widget constructors and callbacks. With Provider you expose a single UserModel that notifies listeners when the name changes so all dependents update automatically.

Analogy
Think of setState as changing a lamp bulb inside one room. Provider is the building's electricity supply that powers many rooms; change it at the source and all rooms notice the difference.
Common mistake

Trying to solve broad data-sharing with only setState and callbacks, which grows error-prone as the app expands.

screens.title: setState() vs Provider pattern
screens.narratorSegment: We'll compare setState and a Provider-based pattern so you can make practical choices. setState belongs in the State object of a StatefulWidget and causes that widget to rebuild. It's simple and low-overhead for UI details like animation controllers, local form inputs, or ephemeral flags. Provider with ChangeNotifier shifts the data into a model object that lives outside individual widgets. Widgets subscribe to that model and rebuild when notifyListeners is called. Concrete example: a counter inside one screen can use setState. But if several screens must display and update the same count, Create a CounterModel and expose it with ChangeNotifierProvider. That prevents passing callbacks and values down multiple levels. Performance trade-offs: setState rebuilds a single widget; watch-based listeners trigger rebuilds only where needed. Selector refines this by selecting a small piece of state so unrelated UI doesn't rebuild. Common misconception: Provider replaces setState entirely — it does not. They solve different scopes of problems. Best practice: prefer setState for isolated, short-lived state and Provider for shared state across the widget tree. When in doubt, start with setState and refactor to Provider as shared requirements appear. A quick question to reflect on: is this piece of state used by two or more unrelated widgets? If yes, consider a Provider model.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › setState vs Provider
setState()

Simple, immediate, and intended for local widget state. Triggers a rebuild of the owning widget.

When to use
  • Local form field values.
  • Short-lived UI flags and animations.
  • Controls that don't affect other parts of the app.
Example
A toggle that shows or hides a single subtree inside a page.
Provider + ChangeNotifier

A model lives outside widgets and notifies listeners when it changes. Ideal for sharing state across many widgets without prop drilling.

When to use
  • Cross-screen state such as user profile or cart contents.
  • Data that multiple widgets must both read and update.
  • When separation of concerns improves testability and reuse.
Example
A CartModel provided at the root so product tiles, cart screen, and checkout all reflect the same items.
Performance note

When using Provider, prefer context.read for event handlers and context.watch or Consumer inside build methods. Use Selector when you need to rebuild only on a specific sub-value change to avoid unnecessary rebuilds.

screens.title: Provider, ChangeNotifier, and notifyListeners
screens.narratorSegment: Here we define the core primitives used in this chapter so you can reason about their roles. ChangeNotifier is a simple class you extend to build observable models. It exposes notifyListeners, which you call after mutating internal state. When notifyListeners is invoked, any widget listening through Provider, Consumer, Selector, or context. watch rebuilds. ChangeNotifierProvider is a Provider variant that creates and, when appropriate, disposes the ChangeNotifier instance for you. Provider itself is a wrapper around InheritedWidget that efficiently supplies objects down the widget tree. Concrete example: a CounterModel extends ChangeNotifier, stores a private count, exposes a getter and methods increment and decrement that update the private value and call notifyListeners. This pattern decouples UI from data logic, letting you test the model separately. A common misconception is that ChangeNotifier enforces immutability — it does not. You must manage internal state carefully and call notifyListeners after changes. Also avoid directly mutating provided objects from outside expected APIs; prefer model methods so notifyListeners is always called correctly. The takeaway: ChangeNotifier is the observable engine, Provider supplies it, and notifyListeners is the signal that tells Flutter which listeners must rebuild. Can you identify a small model in your app to convert into a ChangeNotifier?

keyIdea.title: Notifier contract
keyIdea.text: ChangeNotifier + Provider form a clear contract: mutate state in model methods, call notifyListeners, and let the UI listen and rebuild.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Provider & ChangeNotifier
ChangeNotifier anatomy
// CounterModel extends ChangeNotifier
class CounterModel extends ChangeNotifier {
  int _count = 0;

  int get count => _count;

  void increment() {
    _count++;
    notifyListeners();
  }

  void decrement() {
    _count--;
    notifyListeners();
  }
}
This example shows the pattern: private backing field, public getter, mutating methods that call notifyListeners so the UI gets updates.
Provider responsibility

ChangeNotifierProvider constructs the model and inserts it into the widget tree. When created with create, Provider disposes the model automatically when removed from the tree.

Lifecycle note
If you create a ChangeNotifier yourself and pass it to a Provider.value, you must manage its disposal manually to avoid memory leaks.
Misconception check

Do not assume ChangeNotifier is thread-safe or immutable. Keep state modifications in model methods and always call notifyListeners to keep widgets in sync.

screens.title: Ways to consume provided state
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how widgets read and listen to provided state is essential to building efficient Flutter UIs. There are four common consumption methods. First, context. watch () is used inside a build method to make the widget listen to changes in T; when notifyListeners runs, the widget rebuilds. Use it for UI that must react immediately to state updates. Second, context. read () accesses the provided object without establishing a listener, so it's appropriate inside event handlers like button callbacks where you want to call a method but not have the widget rebuild. Third, Consumer is a widget that takes a builder and rebuilds only the subtree inside the builder when the model changes; use it when you want to limit rebuild scope. Fourth, Selector extracts a specific sub-value S from T and only rebuilds when that selected value changes. This is useful for performance when models are large but only a small value matters to a given widget. Concrete example: a list screen can use context. watch for the list length, Selector for a single task's completed flag, and context. read in the onPressed of a delete icon. Common mistakes include using context. watch inside callbacks or over-wrapping many widgets in Consumers unnecessarily. The takeaway: pick the smallest listening surface necessary—watch or Consumer for UI, read for handlers, and Selector to avoid unwanted rebuilds. Which consumption pattern will reduce rebuilds in your layout?

keyIdea.title: Select minimal listeners
keyIdea.text: Use watch/Consumer for UI that must rebuild, read for handlers, and Selector to scope rebuilds to precise sub-values.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Consume patterns
context.watch
Listens and rebuilds

Use in build when the widget must reflect model changes automatically.

context.read
Access without listening

Use in onPressed or event handlers to call model methods without subscribing to updates.

Consumer
Scoped rebuilds

Wrap a small subtree to control which part of the UI rebuilds when the model changes.

Selector

Selector extracts a value from a model and only rebuilds when that selected value changes. This reduces unnecessary rebuilds when your model contains many fields but the widget cares about one.

Example
Use Selector to watch a boolean completed flag for a single list tile so only that tile rebuilds when toggled.
Anti-pattern
Using watch inside an onPressed handler or wrapping large regions in Consumers indiscriminately.

screens.title: Counter example: model, provider, and consumer
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the canonical counter example implemented with Provider. First you create a CounterModel that extends ChangeNotifier and includes a private count, a getter, and increment and decrement methods that call notifyListeners. This isolates state and update logic. Next you provide this model at the app root with ChangeNotifierProvider so a single instance is shared by all descendants. Finally the UI reads the count using context. watch inside build and calls model methods in button handlers with context. read. A concrete snippet shows how main wraps MyApp with ChangeNotifierProvider and how CounterScreen uses context. watch to display the numeric value. A misconception to avoid: calling context. watch inside an onPressed incorrectly — use context. read in handlers. Also avoid creating a new model instance in a widget's build method; that creates multiple independent models. The practical benefit: pressing increment calls the model's increment, which updates the backing field and calls notifyListeners, and any listening widgets rebuild to show the new count. Try this refactor mentally: replace existing setState counter with CounterModel and observe how multiple widgets can now show the same count without prop drilling. Your takeaway: isolate state in models, provide them once, and consume with the minimal listening surface.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Counter example
Model (lib/models/counter_model.dart)
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

class CounterModel extends ChangeNotifier {
  int _count = 0;

  int get count => _count;

  void increment() {
    _count++;
    notifyListeners();
  }

  void decrement() {
    _count--;
    notifyListeners();
  }
}
Provider (lib/main.dart)
void main() {
  runApp(
    ChangeNotifierProvider(
      create: (context) => CounterModel(),
      child: const MyApp(),
    ),
  );
}
Consume (lib/screens/counter_screen.dart)
final counter = context.watch<CounterModel>();

// UI shows counter.count
// Buttons call:
context.read<CounterModel>().increment();
context.read<CounterModel>().decrement();
This pattern keeps UI code simple: watch for display, read for actions. Avoid using watch inside event handlers.

screens.title: Providing models and lifecycle concerns
screens.narratorSegment: Where you place providers determines the scope and lifetime of your models, so let's cover placement best practices and lifecycle details. If many screens need shared state throughout the app, provide models at the root by wrapping MyApp or the MaterialApp home with ChangeNotifierProvider. This ensures a single instance is available to all descendants. When several models are needed, use MultiProvider to list them cleanly. Example: provide both ToDoListModel and UserProfileModel via MultiProvider at the app root. Regarding disposal, when you create a ChangeNotifier inside ChangeNotifierProvider using its create callback, Provider will dispose the notifier for you when the provider is removed. However, if you supply an existing instance with Provider. value or create the model outside of create, you must manage disposal manually to avoid memory leaks. A common misconception is that ChangeNotifierProvider always manages disposal; that is only true when the provider creates the instance. Also avoid creating providers inside build methods that run frequently, because that can create new instances unexpectedly. The practical takeaway: provide long-lived models at a high level with create, use MultiProvider for multiple models, and be explicit about disposal when you manage instances yourself. Consider which models in your app should live for the app lifetime versus those tied to a specific screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Provider placement
Provide at root for app-wide state
runApp(
  ChangeNotifierProvider(
    create: (context) => ToDoListModel(),
    child: const MyApp(),
  ),
);
Root placement gives a single shared instance to all descendants, ideal for user/session data or global lists.
MultiProvider
MultiProvider(
  providers: [
    ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => ToDoListModel()),
    ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => UserProfileModel()),
  ],
  child: const MyApp(),
)
Disposal note

If you use ChangeNotifierProvider with create, Provider disposes the model automatically. If you instantiate a model yourself and pass it with Provider.value or store it in a field, then call dispose on it when it's no longer needed to prevent leaks.

Mistake to avoid
Providing models inside build methods or creating new instances repeatedly leads to multiple models and unexpected behavior.

keyIdea.title: Activity steps
keyIdea.text: Define Task and ToDoListModel, provide the model at app root, consume with Consumer or watch, and use read for event handlers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › To-Do Activity
Step 1 - Task model
class Task {
  String title;
  bool isCompleted;

  Task({required this.title, this.isCompleted = false});

  void toggleComplete() {
    isCompleted = !isCompleted;
  }
}
Step 2 - ToDoListModel
class ToDoListModel extends ChangeNotifier {
  final List<Task> _tasks = [];
  List<Task> get tasks => _tasks;

  void addTask(String title) {
    _tasks.add(Task(title: title));
    notifyListeners();
  }

  void toggleTaskCompletion(int index) { ... }
}
Step 3 - Provide
Wrap your app with ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => ToDoListModel()). Use MultiProvider if you need more models.
Step 4 - Consume and UI tips
  • Use Consumer or context.watch to rebuild the ListView when tasks change.
  • Use context.read inside FloatingActionButton onPressed to add tasks.
  • Use Selector for individual tiles to avoid rebuilding the entire list.

screens.title: Common mistakes, debugging, and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Let's review the common mistakes you'll encounter and how to debug them. Mistake one is forgetting to call notifyListeners after changing model state. The symptom is that your UI does not update even though the model's internal data changed. Debug by adding logs inside model methods and ensure notifyListeners runs after mutation. Mistake two is using context. watch within event handlers; watch subscribes during build and is inappropriate for callbacks — use context. read in handlers. Mistake three is creating providers inside frequently executed build methods which creates new model instances repeatedly; instead provide models at a stable ancestor using create. For debugging, Flutter DevTools has a Provider tab that shows active providers and can help you spot multiple instances. Performance tips include using Selector to limit rebuilds to the exact sub-value you care about, and preferring Consumer for small rebuild scopes instead of rebuilding large widget subtrees. Also be mindful of lifecycle: if you did not use create, remember to dispose your ChangeNotifier. A pragmatic practice is to keep model methods small, ensure they call notifyListeners only after batch updates, and write unit tests for model logic so UI tests focus on rendering. The final takeaway: instrument your model methods with simple logging, follow the read/watch contract, and place providers at stable, appropriate scopes to avoid lifecycle and performance issues. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Mistakes & Debugging
Forgot notifyListeners
Symptom: UI doesn't update. Fix: call notifyListeners after mutations; add debug prints to confirm execution path.
Using watch in handlers
Watch is for build. Use read in onPressed and other callbacks to avoid build-time subscription errors.
Provider instantiation errors
Creating providers in build creates new instances. Provide at stable ancestors and use create to let Provider manage disposal.
DevTools tip

Use Flutter DevTools Provider tab to inspect active providers and their values. This quickly reveals duplicate instances and lifecycle anomalies.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's close by reinforcing the three most important concepts. First, state scope: recognize when state is local and when it must be shared. Use setState for localized UI concerns and adopt a Provider-based model when multiple widgets need the same data. Second, the Provider pattern: provide a ChangeNotifier at an appropriate ancestor, mutate state in model methods, and call notifyListeners after updates so listeners rebuild. Third, consume smartly: use context. watch or Consumer in build for reactive UI, context. read in event handlers, and Selector to rebuild only when a particular sub-value changes. Common mistakes include forgetting notifyListeners, misusing watch in callbacks, and creating providers in build methods. The practical habit is to centralize shared state, keep model APIs small and testable, and apply minimal listening surfaces for better performance. These practices will make your Flutter apps easier to maintain, test, and extend. Which of these three concepts will you apply first in your next refactor?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Final Reminders

Notify reliably

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll make sense of application state and why a simple setState call becomes fragile as apps grow. State means any data that changes while your app runs and that affects what the user sees. setState is fine for local widget state, but when several widgets need the same data, passing values down repeatedly, also called prop drilling, makes code hard to follow and maintain. Provider offers a lightweight, Flutter-friendly approach built on InheritedWidget. You define a model that extends ChangeNotifier, make it available with a Provider placed higher in the tree, and read or watch that model in descendant widgets. This pattern separates UI from business logic and helps you avoid duplicated updates or tangled callbacks. For example, a counter model exposes a count and increment method; the UI listens for changes and rebuilds when notifyListeners is called. A common pitfall is forgetting notifyListeners or using read where you need watch. Over this chapter you'll learn ChangeNotifier structure, Provider placement, Consumer and Selector use, and a hands-on to-do app. By the end you will be able to choose Provider for moderate complexity apps and understand when finer-grained tools might be required. How could this pattern clean up one of your own widgets?

These learning objectives will guide our work with Provider and ChangeNotifier. First, you'll explain why effective state management is necessary beyond setState, identifying where prop drilling and duplicated update logic create bugs. This objective matters because recognizing when to centralize state helps you choose the right pattern early. Second, you'll understand Provider's core principles: that Provider wraps an InheritedWidget, that ChangeNotifier is the observable model, and that Provider exposes instances to descendants. A concrete example is creating a CounterModel and observing how a single provider instance updates several widgets. Third, you'll implement ChangeNotifier to model observable data, including calling notifyListeners after state changes. This skill is essential to write models that correctly trigger UI rebuilds. Finally, you'll use Provider, Consumer, Selector, and context. watch/read to react to changes efficiently and avoid unnecessary rebuilds. For instance, Selector allows you to rebuild a specific widget only when a selected piece of state changes, improving performance. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress and fix common mistakes like forgetting notifyListeners or using read in a build method.

These objectives continue toward practical mastery. You'll build a simple app demonstrating data flow and state updates using Provider. The hands-on to-do app teaches how to define a Task model, a ToDoListModel that extends ChangeNotifier, and how to update the UI with Consumer and context. read. A concrete example: adding a task calls addTask which modifies the internal list and then notifyListeners, triggering any listening list views to rebuild. You will also learn lifecycle concerns: when ChangeNotifier is created by ChangeNotifierProvider using create, Provider disposes it automatically; when you manage it yourself you must dispose to prevent memory leaks. We'll cover MultiProvider when you need two or more models simultaneously. Finally, common mistakes are emphasized: using context. watch inside an event handler, which leads to incorrect behavior, or creating multiple instances of the same model instead of reusing a single provided instance. Each objective maps to a verified milestone so you can self-check. Practice will include adding, toggling, and removing tasks, and using context. read for event handlers. Which small feature will you implement first in your practice app?

Let's define application state and examine why local setState quickly becomes fragile. State is any data that can change while the app runs and that affects the UI: user input, network results, theme toggles, or a shopping cart. Local state lives inside a single StatefulWidget and can be handled with setState. But when the same data is needed by many widgets at different depths, passing values and callbacks down the tree — called prop drilling — creates tightly coupled components. This coupling makes maintenance harder, testing more painful, and refactors risky because many widgets rely on the same plumbing. Consider a user profile name that must appear in the app bar, a settings page, and a drawer; updating it via setState alone forces you to bubble callbacks through several layers. A centralized observable model solves this by providing a single source of truth. Concrete example: replacing multiple setState callbacks with a ChangeNotifier model that holds the name and calls notifyListeners when it updates. Misconception to check: setState is not inherently bad — it is the right tool for local widget state such as animations or temporary form field values. The key takeaway: use setState for local concerns and choose a Provider-style pattern when state is shared across unrelated widgets, to reduce duplication and make updates predictable. Which piece of your app would be easier to refactor with a central model?

We'll compare setState and a Provider-based pattern so you can make practical choices. setState belongs in the State object of a StatefulWidget and causes that widget to rebuild. It's simple and low-overhead for UI details like animation controllers, local form inputs, or ephemeral flags. Provider with ChangeNotifier shifts the data into a model object that lives outside individual widgets. Widgets subscribe to that model and rebuild when notifyListeners is called. Concrete example: a counter inside one screen can use setState. But if several screens must display and update the same count, Create a CounterModel and expose it with ChangeNotifierProvider. That prevents passing callbacks and values down multiple levels. Performance trade-offs: setState rebuilds a single widget; watch-based listeners trigger rebuilds only where needed. Selector refines this by selecting a small piece of state so unrelated UI doesn't rebuild. Common misconception: Provider replaces setState entirely — it does not. They solve different scopes of problems. Best practice: prefer setState for isolated, short-lived state and Provider for shared state across the widget tree. When in doubt, start with setState and refactor to Provider as shared requirements appear. A quick question to reflect on: is this piece of state used by two or more unrelated widgets? If yes, consider a Provider model.

Here we define the core primitives used in this chapter so you can reason about their roles. ChangeNotifier is a simple class you extend to build observable models. It exposes notifyListeners, which you call after mutating internal state. When notifyListeners is invoked, any widget listening through Provider, Consumer, Selector, or context. watch rebuilds. ChangeNotifierProvider is a Provider variant that creates and, when appropriate, disposes the ChangeNotifier instance for you. Provider itself is a wrapper around InheritedWidget that efficiently supplies objects down the widget tree. Concrete example: a CounterModel extends ChangeNotifier, stores a private count, exposes a getter and methods increment and decrement that update the private value and call notifyListeners. This pattern decouples UI from data logic, letting you test the model separately. A common misconception is that ChangeNotifier enforces immutability — it does not. You must manage internal state carefully and call notifyListeners after changes. Also avoid directly mutating provided objects from outside expected APIs; prefer model methods so notifyListeners is always called correctly. The takeaway: ChangeNotifier is the observable engine, Provider supplies it, and notifyListeners is the signal that tells Flutter which listeners must rebuild. Can you identify a small model in your app to convert into a ChangeNotifier?

Understanding how widgets read and listen to provided state is essential to building efficient Flutter UIs. There are four common consumption methods. First, context. watch () is used inside a build method to make the widget listen to changes in T; when notifyListeners runs, the widget rebuilds. Use it for UI that must react immediately to state updates. Second, context. read () accesses the provided object without establishing a listener, so it's appropriate inside event handlers like button callbacks where you want to call a method but not have the widget rebuild. Third, Consumer is a widget that takes a builder and rebuilds only the subtree inside the builder when the model changes; use it when you want to limit rebuild scope. Fourth, Selector extracts a specific sub-value S from T and only rebuilds when that selected value changes. This is useful for performance when models are large but only a small value matters to a given widget. Concrete example: a list screen can use context. watch for the list length, Selector for a single task's completed flag, and context. read in the onPressed of a delete icon. Common mistakes include using context. watch inside callbacks or over-wrapping many widgets in Consumers unnecessarily. The takeaway: pick the smallest listening surface necessary—watch or Consumer for UI, read for handlers, and Selector to avoid unwanted rebuilds. Which consumption pattern will reduce rebuilds in your layout?

We'll walk through the canonical counter example implemented with Provider. First you create a CounterModel that extends ChangeNotifier and includes a private count, a getter, and increment and decrement methods that call notifyListeners. This isolates state and update logic. Next you provide this model at the app root with ChangeNotifierProvider so a single instance is shared by all descendants. Finally the UI reads the count using context. watch inside build and calls model methods in button handlers with context. read. A concrete snippet shows how main wraps MyApp with ChangeNotifierProvider and how CounterScreen uses context. watch to display the numeric value. A misconception to avoid: calling context. watch inside an onPressed incorrectly — use context. read in handlers. Also avoid creating a new model instance in a widget's build method; that creates multiple independent models. The practical benefit: pressing increment calls the model's increment, which updates the backing field and calls notifyListeners, and any listening widgets rebuild to show the new count. Try this refactor mentally: replace existing setState counter with CounterModel and observe how multiple widgets can now show the same count without prop drilling. Your takeaway: isolate state in models, provide them once, and consume with the minimal listening surface.

Where you place providers determines the scope and lifetime of your models, so let's cover placement best practices and lifecycle details. If many screens need shared state throughout the app, provide models at the root by wrapping MyApp or the MaterialApp home with ChangeNotifierProvider. This ensures a single instance is available to all descendants. When several models are needed, use MultiProvider to list them cleanly. Example: provide both ToDoListModel and UserProfileModel via MultiProvider at the app root. Regarding disposal, when you create a ChangeNotifier inside ChangeNotifierProvider using its create callback, Provider will dispose the notifier for you when the provider is removed. However, if you supply an existing instance with Provider. value or create the model outside of create, you must manage disposal manually to avoid memory leaks. A common misconception is that ChangeNotifierProvider always manages disposal; that is only true when the provider creates the instance. Also avoid creating providers inside build methods that run frequently, because that can create new instances unexpectedly. The practical takeaway: provide long-lived models at a high level with create, use MultiProvider for multiple models, and be explicit about disposal when you manage instances yourself. Consider which models in your app should live for the app lifetime versus those tied to a specific screen.
